raw.abstractText:
Background

 Fibrotic liver is one of the serious pathophysiological consequences of chronic injury to the liver, may progress toward serious complications including cirrhosis and hepatic carcinoma.

Objectives

Panax notoginseng is used for both therapeutic and prophylactic purposes in TCM; it is a source of Dencichine, an active substance that has been proven to exhibit antifibrotic properties in hepatic fibrosis. The present study investigated how Dencichine treatment ameliorates liver fibrosis using an animal model and a cellular fibrosis model.

Methods

Randomly assigned, male C57BL/6J mice received 10% CCl4 for 15 consecutive weeks to induce hepatic fibrosis. Treatment with Dencichine was initiated from 7th week onward. To simulate in-vitro the presence of a fibrotic microenvironment, LX-2 cells were treated with PDGF-BB at a concentration of 20 ng/mL and incubated from one up to four days and then treated by various doses of Dencichine. Liver function was evaluated by measuring alanine aminotransferase (ALT), AST, HA and LN. Histopathology was evaluated by haematoxylin/eosin (HE), Masson's trichrome and Sirius red stains. Quantitative real-time PCR and western blot analyses were used to evaluate mRNA and protein expression levels, respectively. Wound-healing assays and transwell chamber experiments were used to assess cell migration; EdU proliferation detection and flow cytometry were performed to measure cell proliferation and cell cycle, respectively.

Results

 The most important results are a considerable reduction of serum concentrations of AST and ALT, HA and laminin in CCl4-treated mice decreased liver injury and ECM deposition. Furthermore, this compound downregulated the expression of cyclin D1 and cyclin E1 and blocked the activation of PI3K and AKT kinases in fibrotic liver cells.

Conclusion

These results indicate that Dencichine may slow the development of liver fibrosis by interfering with the PI3K-AKT signaling cascade, demonstrating significant anti-scarring properties.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Tibial transverse osteotomy (TTO) is a promising but limited surgical option for diabetic foot (DF). Berberine, a natural compound from Coptis chinensis, exhibits anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic effects relevant to metabolic diseases.

Objectives

This study aimed to evaluate whether adjunctive berberine enhances the therapeutic outcomes of TTO in DF patients and to explore its potential association with the platelet-derived growth factor-B (PDGF-B)/PDGF receptor-β (PDGFRβ) signaling pathway.

Methods

This was a prospective, single-center, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, blinded trial. Of 200 screened DF patients, 96 eligible participants (Wagner grade 2-4) scheduled for TTO were randomized 1:1 to receive either TTO plus local berberine injections (n=48) or TTO plus local saline placebo (n=48). An additional non-randomized diabetic reference group (n=10) and healthy control group (n=10) were included for exploratory cellular studies only. The primary outcome was the total effective rate of ulcer healing at 3 months. Secondary outcomes included changes in Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI), ulcer area, Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain score and serum inflammatory markers (hs-CRP, IL-6). Exploratory outcomes comprised serum VEGF, bFGF and PDGF-B levels, as well as fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue.

Results

All 96 randomized participants completed the 3-month follow-up, with no dropouts. The berberine group demonstrated a significantly higher total effective rate than the surgery-alone group (87.5% vs. 68.8%; risk difference, 18.7%; 95% CI, 1.2% to 36.2%; P < 0.05). At 3 months, the berberine group also showed greater improvements in ABI (mean difference, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.08 to 0.18; P < 0.01) and ulcer healing rate (mean difference, 16.7%; 95% CI, 9.5% to 23.9%; P < 0.01), along with more significant reductions in hs-CRP and IL-6. Berberine treatment was associated with reduced fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue (mean difference, -1.10%; 95% CI, -1.56% to -0.64%; P = 0.001) and lower protein expression of PDGF-B and PDGFRβ. No severe adverse events related to berberine injections were reported.

Conclusion

In DF patients undergoing TTO, adjunctive local berberine therapy significantly improves the total effective rate and promotes ulcer healing, with benefits associated with reduced inflammation and fibroblast apoptosis and downregulation of the PDGF-B/PDGFRβ pathway. These findings are correlative and require further mechanistic validation. Larger multi-center trials are needed to confirm efficacy and safety.

raw.abstractText: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent the first line of host immune defense against a broad spectrum of microorganisms. Whether naturally occurring or synthetically designed, these small peptides can potently inhibit microbial growth and remain stable under diverse conditions. Our work focuses primarily on the in vitro characterization of AMP features in the context of plant-Botrytis interactions.

raw.abstractText: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) is a powerful reverse genetics tool that enables the transient knockdown of gene expression in plants by exploiting their natural antiviral defense mechanisms. This chapter presents a detailed protocol for applying a Cowpea severe mosaic virus (CPSMV)-based VIGS system to study gene function in soybean (Glycine max), with a focus on symbiotic root nodulation. VIGS allows systemic silencing of target genes, making it especially valuable to study pathways involving systemic signaling. The protocol includes Agrobacterium-mediated propagation of CPSMV variants in Nicotiana benthamiana, followed by mechanical inoculation of soybean plants and nodulation analysis. Detailed steps for vector construction, viral amplification, plant infection, and downstream molecular and phenotypic analyses are provided. This protocol is reproducible, accessible, and suitable for functional genomics studies in soybean, particularly for genes involved in nodulation but also in other developmental or stress-related processes.

raw.abstractText: This study aimed to explore the processing mechanism of single medicinal herbs in compound prescriptions, compare the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic changes of Yuanhu Zhitong Formula before and after processing, and elucidate its underlying mechanism against gastric ulcers. The results showed that six components, namely, corydaline, coptisine chloride, palmatine, berberine chloride, phellopterin, and imperatorin, exerted anti-ulcer activities. The optimal vinegar-processing parameters for Corydalis yanhusuo were determined as follows: processing temperature of 84°C, vinegar dosage of 37%, and baking time of 35 min. Vinegar-processed Corydalis yanhusuo could accelerate the in vivo distribution of alkaloid components in the formula, elevate the plasma concentration, and prolong the in vivo retention time of coumarin components. The synergistic effects of the two types of active ingredients endow the vinegar-processed Yuanhu Zhitong Formula with significantly superior antigastric ulcer activity compared with the raw formula. Moreover, network pharmacology results revealed that this formula exerts therapeutic effects against gastric ulcers mainly by regulating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. This study clarified the optimal processing technology and the pharmacodynamic material basis of Yuanhu Zhitong Formula against gastric ulcers, confirmed the efficacy-enhancing effect of processing, and provided data support for the formulation of its processing production standards and clinical medication.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Caffeine is consumed for its presumed cognitive benefits, yet controlled studies have repeatedly failed to find effects on inhibitory control. Cross-sectional work suggests that people with elevated attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms may benefit from chronic, moderate caffeine consumption, but whether acute intake improves cognition in proportion to symptom severity has not been tested experimentally.

Aims

We tested whether 250 mg of caffeine improves active inhibition (withholding a prepared response) and reactive inhibition (resolving response conflict), and whether ADHD symptom severity moderates these effects.

Methods

In a preregistered, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, a nonclinical sample of 36 young adults received 250 mg of caffeine or placebo in counterbalanced order, with testing 45 min after ingestion. Active inhibition was assessed with a Go/No-Go task (204 trials), reactive inhibition with an arrow flanker task (200 trials) and symptoms with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale. Mixed-effects models included treatment, symptom severity, their interaction and ten covariates; Bayes factors quantified evidence for the null.

Results

Both tasks produced their benchmark effects (dz = 1.24 and 1.09) and all indices were reliable (split-half r = 0.73-0.98). Caffeine affected neither commission errors (BF01 = 4.98), response criterion (5.14), Go reaction time (2.83), reaction time variability (4.35), flanker reaction time (5.49) nor flanker accuracy (5.09). ADHD symptoms moderated no effect (15 preregistered tests; smallest p = 0.514), yet predicted performance itself (flanker accuracy r = -0.42), indicating that the null is not due to an insensitive measure.

Conclusions

Caffeine produced no acute benefit for either form of inhibition, and ADHD symptoms did not moderate its effects. Bayes factors supported the absence rather than the nondetection of these effects, arguing against an acute improvement of inhibitory control that scales with ADHD symptom severity in nonclinical young adults. Whether this also holds for chronic consumption or for adults with diagnosed ADHD remains to be tested.

raw.abstractText:
Objective

Caffeine could improve cognitive functions, but study protocols usually prohibit drinking coffee before cognitive testing. However, regular coffee consumers may experience withdrawal effects when they cannot drink their habitual coffee, which may impair cognitive performance. Therefore, we tested the effects of overnight coffee abstinence in regular coffee consumers: once allowing to drink their coffee and once not drinking coffee. The cognitive performance was compared with non-regular coffee consumers.

Methods

Thirty regular coffee consumers (RCCs) and 25 non-regular consumers (N-RCCs) took part in this study. RCCs were tested after their habitual morning coffee (c-RCC) and after overnight abstinence (a-RCC); N-RCCs were tested once. A cognitive battery assessed reaction time (RT), processing speed (digit symbol substitution test), working memory, verbal learning/memory and executive function (Stroop). Sleep quality was included as a covariate.

Results

Compared to c-RCC, overnight coffee abstinence significantly slowed RTs but did not affect the performance in the other cognitive tasks. In the a-RCC condition, but not the c-RCC condition, the RTs were slower than those of the N-RCCs, while accuracy measures were comparable across groups. Sleep quality did not alter these findings.

Conclusions

Overnight coffee abstinence selectively slowed RT, and no statistical support was found for effects on memory or executive function. This suggests that overnight coffee abstinence protocols may introduce withdrawal-related RT slowing as a confound in habitual consumers, whereas other cognitive domains may not be affected. Allowing habitual consumers to maintain normal coffee intake could reduce this bias, supporting tailored rather than uniform abstinence requirements based on the specific outcomes studied.

raw.abstractText: The collagen triple helix is the most abundant protein structural motif in animals. It tolerates any amino acid in its Xaa and Yaa positions but demands glycine (Gly) at every third position, where the residue packs into the sterically forbidding core of the triple helix and donates the recurring interstrand N-H⋯OC hydrogen bond that stitches the three strands together. (2S)-Proline (Pro) and (2S,4R)-4-hydroxyproline (Hyp) are enriched far above their proteome-wide abundance because they preorganize individual strands into the polyproline II conformation, lowering the entropic cost of folding. We asked whether the triple helix is intrinsically stable enough to form from strands that carry no such preorganization, that is, from polyglycine. To offset the conformational entropy of a Gly-rich tract, we embedded Gly<sub>6</sub> within flanking triple-helical (Pro-Hyp-Gly)<sub>n</sub> clamps in Ac-(Pro-Hyp-Gly)<sub>6</sub>-Gly<sub>6</sub>-(Pro-Hyp-Gly)<sub>5</sub>-Pro-Hyp-NH<sub>2</sub> and compared it with an otherwise identical peptide in which Gly<sub>6</sub> was replaced by two [2-(2-aminoethoxy)ethoxy]acetic acid units, a flexible, length-matched spacer that lacks most of the regularly spaced backbone amides of Gly<sub>6</sub>. Circular dichroism spectroscopy revealed the diagnostic positive band at 225 nm. The molar ellipticity of the spacer-containing control was 86% of that of the Gly<sub>6</sub>-containing peptide, matching the 35/41 = 85% ratio of residues capable of triple-helix formation and consistent with the Gly<sub>6</sub> segment contributing to the triple-helical signal. Thermal denaturation yielded a T<sub>m</sub> of 46.8°C for the Gly<sub>6</sub>-containing peptide, 6.3°C higher than that of the matched spacer control. This added stability indicates that the polyglycine tract is not merely accommodated within the helix but contributes stabilizing interstrand hydrogen bonds. Together, these data indicate that three polyglycine strands can form a collagen triple helix when flanked by triple-helical clamps. This result is consistent with the idea that the triple-helical architecture predates the recruitment of Pro and Hyp, informs the evolutionary origin of collagen, and offers a blunt-ended, symmetric scaffold for designing peptidic triple helices.

raw.abstractText:
While insulin activates the sympathetic nervous system in experimental settings, whether therapeutic insulin administration is associated with cardiac sympathetic predominance under free-living conditions remains unclear. This prospective observational study investigated the association between insulin dosing and cardiac autonomic balance in adults with type 1 diabetes managed exclusively with insulin therapy. Participants underwent continuous heart rate variability (HRV) and glucose monitoring over 4 consecutive days during routine daily activities. Cardiac sympathetic predominance was assessed using the low-frequency power to high-frequency power (LF/HF) ratio derived from HRV analysis, and associations were evaluated using generalized estimating equations. A higher last bolus insulin dose was associated with an increased LF/HF ratio during the early sleep phase. A higher basal insulin dose was also associated with an increased LF/HF ratio during the late sleep phase. These associations persisted after adjustment for mean glucose and mean absolute glucose change during the corresponding sleep phases. Under free-living conditions, higher insulin doses were associated with dose-dependent increases in cardiac sympathetic predominance, independent of glycemic profiles. These findings suggest that insulin dosing may be linked to cardiac autonomic regulation in individuals with type 1 diabetes, highlighting the importance of considering cardiac autonomic balance and potential cardiovascular risk when optimizing insulin therapy.

Article highlights

The relationship between therapeutic insulin administration and cardiac autonomic balance under free-living conditions remains unclear. We examined whether insulin dosing was associated with cardiac sympathetic predominance during daily life in adults with type 1 diabetes managed with insulin therapy. Higher last bolus and basal insulin doses were associated with increased cardiac sympathetic predominance during the early and late sleep phases, respectively, independent of glycemic profiles. These findings suggest that insulin dosing patterns may be linked to cardiac autonomic balance, with potential implications for optimizing insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Prolonged exposure to hepatotoxic antiretroviral therapy (ART) could lead to chronic liver injury, which might increase risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We used causal inference methods to evaluate if cumulative exposure to ART with known mechanisms of chronic liver injury is associated with HCC among people with HIV (PWH), by chronic liver disease (CLD) status.

Methods

We conducted a cohort study of antiretroviral-naive PWH with and without diagnosed CLD who initiated ART in the Veterans Affairs between 1999 and 2023. Exposure to ART with known mechanism of chronic liver injury (mitochondrial toxicity or accumulation of toxic intermediates) was determined monthly through prescription fills. Incident HCC was identified by Veterans Affairs National Cancer Registry and/or recorded diagnoses. Marginal structural models estimated odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of HCC associated with cumulative exposure to chronic liver injury-inducing ART compared with ART without chronic liver injury mechanisms, by CLD status.

Results

Among 11,854 PWH without CLD and 6771 PWH with CLD, we observed 112 and 378 HCC events, respectively. Among PWH without CLD, ≥4 years of exposure to chronic liver injury-inducing ART was associated with HCC when compared with ≥4 years of use of ART without chronic liver injury mechanisms (OR = 4.02 [95% CI: 1.00-16.24]). Among PWH with CLD, ≥4 years of exposure to chronic liver injury-inducing ART was not associated with HCC (OR = 1.36; 95% CI: 0.68-2.72).

Conclusion

Four or more years of ART with a chronic liver injury mechanism was associated with HCC among PWH without CLD, but not those with CLD.

raw.abstractText: Melatonin (MEL) is an endogenous hormone that regulates circadian rhythm, immune function and oxidative stress responses. Norepinephrine (NE), an endogenous catecholamine, increases blood pressure through the sympathetic nervous system and is commonly administered intraoperatively or in the clinically ill patient for hemodynamic support. Although endogenous NE is known to stimulate MEL synthesis, the effects of exogenous intravenous NE on plasma MEL concentration, particularly under general anaesthesia (GA), remain poorly characterised. This study examined the influence of intravenous NE on plasma MEL concentrations in healthy volunteers, both awake and under general anaesthesia. A secondary analysis was conducted using data from a prospective, single-centre, cross-over study involving volunteers who received stepwise NE infusions while awake and under total intravenous general anaesthesia. raw.abstractText: TYRO3, AXL, and MERTK, the TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), play roles in phagocytosis and negative regulation of immune responses, contributing to homeostasis in many adult tissues. Aberrant TAM signaling leads to diseases including autoimmune disorders, viral infection, inflammation, and cancer. Development of successful drugs targeting TAM receptors is hindered by incomplete knowledge of the receptor activation mechanism. Receptor dimerization is assumed to play a role, as seen for most RTKs. However, full biological responses require the TAM ligands to engage phosphatidylserine in an opposing cell or virus membrane, suggesting a more complex mechanism, possibly involving higher-order receptor oligomerization or clustering. Here, we present an X-ray crystal structure of the ectodomain of MERTK, which adopts a highly curved conformation with key interdomain boundaries stabilized by N-linked glycan moieties. We show that this MERTK extracellular region (ECR) forms a similar conformation in solution using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), which also suggests a flexible ECR. We compare these crystallographic and solution data for MERTK with SAXS and AlphaFold structural predictions for the other two TAM receptors. SAXS data confirm that each TAM ECR has a distinct curvature, with TYRO3 the most bent and AXL relatively straight. This leads us to speculate that these different ectodomain conformations guide receptor-specific functions. The MERTK X-ray crystal structure also suggests a head-to-tail intermolecular interaction between the Ig2 domain of one MERTK and the FNIIIb domain of a second that has intriguing parallels with interactions that have been proposed to regulate Eph receptor clustering.

raw.abstractText: Activity-guided separation of medicinal plants requires linking activity signals and chromatographic resolution in complex matrices. In this study, based on a previously established HPLC-DPPH platform, medium-pressure prefractionation and preparative chromatographic purification were applied for the targeted isolation of free radical scavengers from Saxifraga tangutica (S. tangutica). Medium-pressure prefractionation reduced sample complexity and enriched active fractions, while Click XION chromatography concentrated the target fraction. Subsequent purification on the ReproSil-Pur C18 AQ column resolved this fraction into two baseline-separated active peaks, affording compounds with purities greater than 95%. The isolated compounds were identified as quercetin-3-O-β-D-glucoside-7-O-β-D-glucoside and quercetin-3-O-β-D-galactoside-7-O-β-D-glucoside, a pair of C-4″-epimeric quercetin 3,7-di-O-glycosides. DFT calculations, molecular docking, and ADMET prediction further supported the comparative interpretation of their electronic features, antioxidant-related interaction potential, and predicted pharmacokinetic profiles. Overall, this study achieved the activity guided isolation and activity evaluation of a pair of high-purity C-4″-epimeric flavonol diglycosides from S. tangutica, providing a practical chromatographic strategy for the targeted characterization of structurally similar bioactive constituents from medicinal plants.

raw.abstractText: Ripened washed-rind and long-ripened cheeses owe their prized sulfurous, savory character to intensive proteolysis and amino-acid catabolism; the same activity, when poorly controlled, also generates sensory off-flavors and toxic biogenic amines (BAs). Histamine and tyramine reach up to approximately 2000-2500 and 1000-2000 mg/kg in extreme samples, although most cheeses contain far less, so that a 30-g portion of a high-histamine cheese can exceed the 50-mg per-meal intake regarded as without adverse effect in healthy adults. Flavor formation and chemical safety have traditionally been studied apart. This critical review reframes them as two outcomes of one metabolism: Proteolysis liberates a shared free amino-acid pool from which volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs) and BAs arise. Because the principal VSCs derive from methionine whereas the major BAs derive from histidine, tyrosine, ornithine, arginine, and lysine, we treat the branches not as direct competitors for one substrate but as metabolically coupled fates linked by shared proteolytic supply, overlapping physicochemical controls and microbial cross-feeding. Integrating evidence across cheese families, we reclassify the ripening microbiota into condition-dependent functional guilds, formalize metabolic bivalence (organisms that both generate flavor and degrade amines), and define a sensory inflection point separating the windowed VSC dose-response from the monotonic BA hazard. We critically appraise multi-omics, volatilomics, biosensors, machine learning, and digital twins, and outline a precision-fermentation roadmap. Current, largely in vitro, and single-variety evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, controllable decoupling, which we frame as a testable hypothesis that recasts cheese quality as a controllable metabolic-allocation problem.

raw.abstractText: Vitamin D is a nutrient and prohormone obtained from diet and supplements and synthesized in the skin. It is essential for calcium and phosphate homeostasis and skeletal health and influences multiple extra-skeletal processes, yet deficiency remains common worldwide. This narrative review summarizes vitamin D sources, physiology, metabolism, pharmacokinetics, clinical relevance and safety and outlines the distinct pharmacokinetic profiles and clinical roles of vitamin D, calcidiol and calcitriol and its analogues. Evidence consistently supports vitamin D, combined with calcium, for preventing and treating deficiency-related skeletal disorders in high-risk populations, and in specific conditions such as malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, hypoparathyroidism and frailty. In vitamin D-replete populations, large trials show limited extra-skeletal benefits, apart from modest effects on cancer mortality and progression from prediabetes to Type 2 diabetes. Untargeted screening is not recommended. Future research should prioritize targeted supplementation, standardized assays and identification of populations most likely to benefit from supplementation.

raw.abstractText: The GABA  B receptor is a central regulator of neuronal transmission and excitability by pre- and postsynaptic mechanisms. Its dysfunction causes severe neurological disease, but the underlying pathomechanisms remain elusive. Here, we exploit a distinct CNS autoimmune disorder in which patients develop specific autoantibodies against GABA  B receptors causing autoimmune encephalitis with severe memory dysfunction and epilepsy. We demonstrate that human autoantibodies target the sushi-domains of the GABA  B receptor B1a subunit and the B2 subunit and interfere with presynaptic signaling. Our results demonstrate that autoimmune presynaptic pathomechanisms alone are sufficient to interfere with memory processing, thus defining a causal link between molecular GABA  B receptor disturbance, synaptic pathology, circuit dysfunction, and dementia distinct from classical neurodegenerative processes.

raw.abstractText: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is an important and significant reason for cancer-related morbidity and mortality globally. Treatment remains challenging due to recurrence, metastasis, and chemoresistance. Evidence shows that oxidative stress, ongoing inflammation, and cancer stem cells (CSCs) play essential functions in CRC development and progression. Nrf2 is a master regulator of cellular redox balance through the Keap1-Nrf2-is signalling pathway. Normal activation of Nrf2 protects colonic cells from oxidative DNA harm and inflammation during initial carcinogenesis. However, sustained Nrf2 activation in tumours encourages chemoresistance, metabolic reprogramming, and CSC upkeep, showing a dual role. Traditional medicine and dietary phytochemicals (curcumin, sulforaphane, resveratrol, EGCG, berberine) can modulate Nrf2 while interacting with NF-κB, Wnt/β-catenin, and Notch pathways. This review synthesises mechanistic and translational evidence on Nrf2 modulation in CRC chemoprevention, stressing conventional medicine-derived agents in modern approaches. It moreover highlights difficulties, limitations, and future viewpoints for precision chemoprevention and personalised interventions.

Introduction

This guideline establishes recommendations for the treatment of SWD.

Methods

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) commissioned a task force of experts in sleep and circadian medicine to develop recommendations and assign strengths based on a systematic review of the literature and an assessment of the evidence using the GRADE process. The task force summarized the relevant literature and the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations supporting the recommendations. The AASM Board of Directors approved the final recommendations.

Recommendations

The following recommendations are intended as a guide for clinicians in choosing specific treatment(s) for symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or insomnia, and for circadian adaptation in adults with SWD. Each recommendation statement is assigned a strength (e.g., "Strong" or "Conditional"). For SWD, there were only "conditional" recommendations for or against (i.e., "We suggest…") and those requiring the clinician to use clinical knowledge and experience and consider the individual patient's values and preferences to determine the best course of action. Interventions in recommendation statements were compared to no treatment. Adults with SWD with symptoms of excessive sleepiness associated with work schedule: 1. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of armodafinil or modafinil taken 30 to 60 minutes prior to the night shift over no armodafinil or modafinil (Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). 2. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Individuals with SWD who exhibit insomnia and daytime function impairments may also benefit from using bright light during their night shift. 3. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of caffeine taken prior to and/or during the night shift over no caffeine (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 4. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of a clockwise rotating shift schedule over a counterclockwise rotating shift schedule (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 5. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests taking a nap over no nap prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Sleep inertia occurring soon after the nap may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleep inertia prior to driving or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 6. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests either not eating or eating a snack rather than eating a full meal during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 7. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of caffeine and bright light over the combination of no caffeine and no bright light (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 8. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of taking a nap and caffeine over the combination of no nap and no caffeine prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia: 9. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia the AASM suggests the use of CBT-I over no CBT-I (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 10. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia following the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 11. In adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia, when transitioning from daytime to nighttime sleep, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin for night sleep following shift work (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 12. In adults with SWD who desire to take a nap prior to the first night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin prior to the nap (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Melatonin may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleepiness prior to driving, returning to work or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 13. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of ramelteon or other melatonin receptor agonists over no melatonin receptor agonist (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 14. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of suvorexant or other dual orexin receptor antagonists over no dual orexin receptor antagonists (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 15. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests against the use of triazolam and other benzodiazepines (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation: 16. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty).

Remark

For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 17. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night and fixed daytime sleep timing over the combination of no bright light and no fixed sleep timing (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 18. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night, fixed daytime sleep timing, and reduced-light-transmittance glasses in the morning over the combination of no bright light, no fixed sleep timing, and no reduced-light-transmittance glasses (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark 1 : For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. Remark 2: Attention to driving safety is important when wearing reduced-light-transmittance glasses. Other considerations for adults with SWD: 19. In adults with SWD who are working either an 8-hour or 12-hour night shift, the AASM does not suggest working one shift duration over the other (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

This recommendation does not consider other shift durations, rotation, or the number of consecutive shifts. This guideline did not look at shift durations exceeding 12 hours. The total number of hours worked per week ranged from 36 to 52.

Background

High-grade (HG) bladder urothelial carcinoma is an aggressive tumor with poor outcomes, underscoring the need for early molecular stratification. However, a comprehensive functional understanding of its metabolic landscape remains limited. This study aims to delineate the proteomic and metabolic hallmarks of HG bladder cancer by leveraging formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue archives.

Methods

We performed integrated proteomic (data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry) and untargeted metabolomic profiling on FFPE specimens from a discovery cohort of 56 patients (27 low-grade/LG, 29 HG). Key findings were validated via immunohistochemistry (IHC) on an independent cohort of 60 patients (30 LG, 30 HG).

Results

Proteomics revealed extensive molecular remodeling in HG tumors, with 2,506 differentially expressed proteins enriched in metabolic pathways. Metabolomics identified 67 altered metabolites, highlighting a profoundly rewired metabolic network. Integrated analysis converged on 2 core pathways: (1) enhanced nucleotide anabolism supported by the upregulation of enzymes including phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), and (2) a collapsed creatine-phosphagen system evidenced by marked decreases in creatine/creatinine. IHC validation confirmed significant upregulation of PHGDH in HG tumors. Intriguingly, while metabolomic and DIA‑MS‑based proteomic data indicated downregulation of guanidinoacetate N‑methyltransferase (GAMT), the terminal enzyme for creatine biosynthesis, IHC on an independent validation cohort demonstrated robust GAMT immunoreactive accumulation within HG tumor cells. This multi‑omics discordance points toward complex, non‑canonical dysregulation consistent with a working model of protein‑catalytic‑function decoupling, which is presented as a testable working model requiring further experimental validation.

Conclusion

This multi-omics study defines a metabolic dichotomy in HG bladder cancer, characterized by concurrent anabolic reinforcement and energy buffer collapse. We validate PHGDH as a consistent biomarker and uncover complex dysregulation of GAMT, consistent with a testable working model involving putative post-translational modifications, protein truncation, aberrant subcellular sequestration, or gain-of-non-canonical functions. Our findings provide novel metabolic biomarkers and reveal an unexpected layer of complexity in the molecular pathology of advanced bladder cancer.

raw.abstractText: GABA is a neurotransmitter and a four-carbon non-protein amino acid that is produced from L-glutamate through an enzymatic decarboxylation reaction catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase (GAD). This amino acid is naturally present in microorganisms, plants, and animals. As a neurotransmitter in the central nervous system of mammals, GABA plays a pivotal role in regulating neuronal excitability and maintaining the balance of neural activity. Growing interest in improving human health and developing functional foods has increased global attention toward GABA, leading to considerable interest in its incorporation and enrichment in food products. Despite the potential health benefits of GABA, endogenous GABA concentrations in many food matrices are relatively low, limiting their potential as dietary sources. Consequently, enrichment strategies, including fermentation, germination, and other bioprocessing approaches, have attracted attention as alternatives to direct GABA addition and may facilitate the development of GABA-enriched functional foods. Overall, this review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding GABA biosynthesis, its physiological functions, and its applications in food products. It also discusses current strategies for GABA enrichment and highlights the factors influencing its production and applications.

raw.abstractText:
Abstract

Intermittent hypoxia associated with obstructive sleep apnea can impair auditory function, but the early mechanisms underlying auditory cortical injury and the extent to which these changes recover after the restoration of normoxia remain unclear. This study investigated the mechanisms underlying auditory cortical injury in a rat model of intermittent hypoxia and evaluated the protective effects of reoxygenation. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats were assigned to control, intermittent hypoxia, intermittent hypoxia followed by 1 week of normoxic recovery, or control followed by normoxic recovery groups. Short-term intermittent hypoxia caused high-frequency hearing loss and increased spontaneous firing in the primary auditory cortex. After 1 week of normoxic recovery, auditory thresholds and cortical firing rates returned to levels comparable to those in the control group. Glutamate levels did not differ significantly among the groups, whereas γ-aminobutyric acid and 5-hydroxytryptamine levels were elevated in the intermittent hypoxia followed by normoxic recovery group. Intermittent hypoxia increased superoxide dismutase activity, reduced catalase activity, and elevated the levels of tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-6. Normoxic recovery normalized catalase activity and reduced tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin-6 levels, whereas superoxide dismutase activity and interleukin- 1β levels remained elevated. Metabolomic analysis identified alterations in unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis, branched-chain amino acid metabolism, ferroptosis-related pathways, redox-related metabolism, and amino acid and protein turnover, several of which persisted after recovery. These findings indicate that acute intermittent hypoxia-induced auditory dysfunction and cortical hyperexcitability are reversible, whereas redox, inflammatory, and metabolic abnormalities recover asynchronously. Persistent molecular disturbances after functional recovery may provide potential targets for further investigation of obstructive sleep apnea-associated central auditory injury.

raw.title: Integrating stool chemistry measurements with metagenomics in adults reveals distinct gut health profiles
raw.authorString: Straub TJ, Nieto PA, Trachsel JM, Sturgeon H, Edwards S, Mayer EA, Mars RA, Sukhum KV, Hoy CS.
raw.abstractText: Stool chemistry metrics, including calprotectin, lactoferrin, and secretory IgA, are used to assess gut inflammation in clinical or research settings. However, these measures in isolation provide a limited view of gut physiology and lack microbial context. Shotgun metagenomics offers a comprehensive assessment of the gut microbiome's taxonomic composition and functional potential, yet its integration with stool chemistry metrics remains underexplored. We analyzed 877 adult stool samples with paired shotgun metagenomic sequencing and chemistry measurements to integrate the microbiome with 12 stool chemistry metrics. Calprotectin, lactoferrin, and secretory IgA were associated with shifts in microbiome composition (beta diversity), while deviations from typical levels of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), including butyrate, were associated with both changes in alpha diversity and microbiome composition. Network analysis revealed two distinct microbial neighborhoods: one associated with higher butyrate and lower calprotectin and lactoferrin and another associated with lower butyrate and higher calprotectin and lactoferrin. Machine learning models trained on taxonomic and functional data showed modest discrimination of stool chemistry states, performing best for SCFA deficiency and less well for host-derived inflammatory metrics. Together, these findings systematically characterize microbiome-stool chemistry relationships across a large paired dataset, providing a framework for interpreting stool chemistry metrics in the context of shotgun metagenomic profiles.

raw.abstractText: Repeated problem-based learning (PBL) sessions are intended to sustain active, collaborative, and self-directed learning, yet evidence is mixed as to whether familiar PBL routines consistently maintain an appropriate level of learner activation over time. This repeated-measures study examined whether embedding a peer-led examination simulation into regular PBL reshapes psychophysiological and achievement-emotional state profiles. Forty-two medical students were assessed during resting reference, regular PBL, and PBL with peer-led examination simulation. Heart rate variability (HRV) was quantified using RMSSD, SDNN, pNN50, and LF/HF, alongside anxiety, perceived stress, achievement emotions, motivation, self-rated performance, and post-session appraisal. Both PBL formats reduced HRV relative to rest, indicating autonomic activation during regular PBL itself. Compared with regular PBL, examination simulation produced additional HRV withdrawal, higher anxiety and perceived stress, and lower boredom. Baseline-adjusted mixed models supported effects for RMSSD and SDNN; pNN50 did not survive false-discovery-rate correction, and LF/HF showed no robust effect. Enjoyment, motivation, and self-rated performance did not differ significantly. Students reported greater perceived benefit from and stronger preference for the simulation format. Peer-led examination simulation thus shifted PBL toward a more salient, assessment-like psychophysiological and emotional state profile.

raw.title: Feasibility study on using the diffusion-weighted imaging liver pulsation artifact as marker of liver fibrosis
raw.authorString: Groß FJ, Guillaume F, Chaudry O, Nguyen T, Abbas I, Bickelhaupt S, Mathy S, Arnold C, Bäuerle T, Fautz H, Hellwig K, Uder M, Saake M, Laun F.
raw.abstractText:
Background:

Liver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) often shows signal loss in the left lobe due to cardiac pulsation, known as the pulsation artifact.

Purpose:

This study was conducted to turn this bug into a feature. We hypothesized that the pulsation artifact, caused by mechanically transmitted waves, is influenced by tissue stiffness and, thereby, indicative of cirrhosis in the left liver lobe. Thus, we evaluated the potential of DWI pulsation artifacts to detect liver cirrhosis. Study type: This study included both retrospective patients and prospective healthy volunteers. Study population: Thirteen healthy volunteers, 16 patients with cirrhosis (Ishak 5 or 6), and three patients without cirrhosis (Ishak 0, 1, or 2) were included. Field Strength/Sequence: Imaging was performed at 1.5 T and 3 T using echoplanar DWI of the liver with two b-values, b50 = 50 s/mm2 and b800 = 800 s/mm2. Assessment: After manual segmentation of the left and right liver lobes, 18 first-order features were extracted from b50 and b800 images. We assumed the pulsation artifact was predominantly present in the left liver lobe in the b800 images. Thus, we computed the ratios of the intensity-normalized b800 features obtained from the left and right liver lobes. Additionally, we performed an intensity normalization to address the sometimes different signal intensities of left and right liver lobe. Then, we conducted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis to differentiate cirrhotic from non- cirrhotic livers. Statistical tests: ROC analysis and leave-one-out bootstrapping were applied, both yielding area under the curve (AUC) values.

Results:

Left liver pulsation artifacts were more pronounced in non-cirrhotic livers and largely absent in cirrhotic livers. The first quartile feature, i.e. the first quartile of the normalized signal, best distinguished cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers (AUC = 0.95; 95% confidence interval 0.87–1.00). Data conclusion: The left liver DWI pulsation artifact reflects liver stiffness and could serve as a simple, intrinsic marker of liver cirrhosis. Analysis of the signal magnitude can differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers.

papers.title: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C) Attenuates Dichlorvos-Induced Neurobehavioral and Oxido-Inflammatory Stress in Discrete Brain Regions

raw.title: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C) Attenuates Dichlorvos-Induced Neurobehavioral and Oxido-Inflammatory Stress in Discrete Brain Regions
raw.authorString: Ogbuokiri DK, Abugu JI, Oladosu OB, Unekwuojo IB, Agufusi NP, Kenechukwu EV.
raw.abstractText:
Background:

Dichlorvos is a widely used organophosphate pesticide associated with neurotoxicity through acetylcholinesterase inhibition, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. Chronic exposure may cause neuronal dysfunction and structural brain alterations. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C), a potent antioxidant, may provide neuroprotection against oxidative damage. This study evaluated the protective effects of ascorbic acid against dichlorvos—induced neurobehavioral and oxido—inflammatory alterations in adult male Wistar rats.

Methods:

Thirty—six rats were randomly assigned into six groups (n = 6): control, dichlorvos (20 mg/kg), dichlorvos plus low—dose ascorbic acid (50 mg/kg), low—dose ascorbic acid, dichlorvos plus high-dose ascorbic acid (150 mg/kg), and high—dose ascorbic acid groups. Treatments were administered orally for six weeks. Neurobehavioral performance was assessed using the T—maze and hanging—wire tests. Oxidative stress biomarkers, including malondialdehyde, superoxide dismutase, and catalase, were evaluated in the hippocampus and amygdala. Histological examinations of the hippocampus, cerebellum, and prefrontal cortex were also performed. Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test ().

Results:

No significant difference in brain weight was observed across groups. Neurobehavioral assessments showed no statistically significant differences between pre— and post—treatment performances, although dichlorvos exposure produced a slight decline, while ascorbic acid—treated groups showed dose—dependent improvement. Dichlorvos significantly increased malondialdehyde levels and decreased superoxide dismutase and catalase activities compared with control (p < 0.05). Co—administration of ascorbic acid significantly reduced lipid peroxidation and improved antioxidant enzyme activities relative to the dichlorvos group (p <0.05). Histologically, the hippocampus remained largely preserved, while mild neuronal degeneration was observed in the prefrontal cortex of dichlorvos—treated rats. The cerebellum showed mostly normal architecture, with mild molecular layer degeneration in the high—dose dichlorvos plus ascorbic acid group.

Conclusions:

Ascorbic acid attenuated dichlorvos—induced oxidative stress and reduced associated histopathological alterations, with limited but observable improvements in neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings suggest its potential protective role against organophosphate—induced neurotoxicity.

raw.abstractText: Vitamin C may be important for maintaining skeletal muscle health and preventing sarcopenia, but most previous epidemiological studies have investigated dietary intakes rather than vitamin C status. To address this gap, this study investigated cross-sectional associations between both plasma and dietary vitamin C and muscle strength and physical performance. This study analysed data from over 5000 participants of the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC)-Norfolk cohort (aged 48-92 years). Multivariable linear regression models, adjusted for lifestyle, biological, medical, and dietary covariates, were used to investigate associations between dietary (categorised as quintiles, Qs) and plasma vitamin C (low < 25μmol/L, suboptimal 25 to < 50μmol/L, optimal ≥ 50μmol/L), and handgrip strength (adjusted for height: HGS<sub>ht</sub>), gait speed, and 5-chair-stand time. Least square means for outcome measures were calculated from regression models. Women with optimal versus low plasma vitamin C had higher HGS<sub>ht</sub> (+ 0.54 kg/m<sup>2</sup>, p = 0.009), and faster gait speed and chair-stand time (+ 0.11m/s, p < 0.001; - 1.03s, p = 0.028, respectively). Men with optimal versus low plasma vitamin C had faster gait speed and chair-stand time (+ 0.05m/s, p = 0.01; - 0.71s, p = 0.026, respectively). Compared with Q1 of dietary intake, women in Q2 and Q5 had faster gait speed (+ 0.04m/s, p < 0.01 for both); women in Q4 and Q5 had faster chair-stand times (- 0.67s, p = 0.002; - 0.57s, p = 0.013, respectively). No associations were found for dietary vitamin C in men. These findings suggest that maintaining optimal plasma vitamin C status could be important for maintaining physical function. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to support our findings.

We evaluated pakchoi growth and legacy P utilization in an acidified, P-enriched greenhouse soil, comparing an unfertilized, unamended control (CK) with equal-carbon inputs of low-C:P, high-P chicken manure (OF) and high-C:P, low-P plant-derived amendments: alkali lignin (AL), straw (ST), and alkali-lignin-modified straw (AST). Compared with the OF, shoot dry weight was 47.0% and 12.4% higher under ST and AST, respectively, while shoot P uptake increased by 80.2% and 76.8%. OF produced an apparent P surplus, whereas ST and AST generated negative apparent P balances, indicating current-season amendment P inputs could not offset shoot P removal and supporting enhanced legacy P utilization without further accumulation of available or labile inorganic P. Plant-derived amendments increased soil C:P and pH, generally enhanced C- and N-acquiring enzyme activities, and reduced ecoenzymatic vector angles, alleviating relative microbial P-acquisition limitation. Metagenomic and random forest analyses showed that enhanced P acquisition was not primarily linked to a single P-cycling process, but more closely associated with resource stoichiometry and soluble N status, alongside coordinated restructuring of microbial C degradation, N transformation, and P-cycling functions. Overall, AL most strongly ameliorated acidity but elicited weak plant responses; ST produced the strongest biomass response, while AST maintained comparably high P acquisition and markedly improved soil pH. These high-C:P amendments provide a low-P alternative to high-P manure inputs, offering a strategy for reduced-P management and legacy P utilization.

In this study, zebrafish were used as a model and exposed to butylparaben at concentrations of 0, 1, 1.5, and 2 mg/L from 10 to 72 hpf. This study demonstrates that butylparaben exerts developmental and immunotoxic effects in zebrafish, providing experimental evidence for the environmental safety assessment of this class of preservatives.

raw.abstractText: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibits profound clinical heterogeneity; however, its underlying neurobiological substrates remain unclear. Here, leveraging large – scale structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 12,663 typically developing children and 1,699 children with ADHD across Chinese and United States cohorts, we construct population specific pediatric brain charts via hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling to quantify individual deviations in cortical morphology. Data-driven clustering identifies two robust, cross – ethnically replicable ADHD biotypes: an infra – normal biotype characterized by widespread cortical thinning and a supra – normal biotype marked by cortical thickening. Multivariate analyses reveal distinct brain–behavior architectures: cortical deviations correlate preferentially with symptom severity in the infra–normal biotype but with both symptom severity and cognitive performance in the supranormal biotype. Clinically, the infra–normal biotype demonstrates a superior response to methylphenidate over atomoxetine, whereas the supra–normal biotype responds comparably to both. Transcriptomic analyses identify biotype–specific molecular signatures converging with ADHD genome–wide association study (GWAS) risk loci but exhibiting distinct expression patterns in the brain. These findings classify ADHD heterogeneity into neurobiologically distinct, clinically informed biotypes, providing a mechanistic framework for precision psychiatry in pediatric ADHD.

raw.abstractText:
Introduction and aim

Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, and a substantial proportion of patients have drug-resistant disease or experience adverse effects from anticonvulsant medications. Berberine, a blood-brain-barrier-permeant isoquinoline alkaloid, has shown anticonvulsant potential in preclinical models. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the preclinical evidence on berberine's anticonvulsant efficacy, its dose-response and formulation dependence, and its mechanisms of action.

Methodology

PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library were searched and reported per PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420251135006). Random-effects models (DerSimonian-Laird with Hartung-Knapp adjustment) pooled dichotomous outcomes as risk ratios (RR) and continuous outcomes as standardised mean differences (SMD); pre-specified subgroup, dose-response, leave-one-out and GRADE analyses were conducted.

Results

Sixteen studies were included. Berberine reduced the incidence of status epilepticus/generalised seizure (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.61-0.87; I2 = 35%), the proportion reaching the fully kindled state (RR 0.53, 0.37-0.75; I2 = 0%) and seizure-related mortality (RR 0.72, 0.60-0.85; I2 = 0%), with a trend toward fewer spontaneous recurrent seizures (RR 0.65, 0.40-1.04). Seizure severity decreased (SMD 3.09, 1.45-4.74) and latency increased (SMD 1.50, 0.23-2.76). A monotonic dose-response gradient was observed across ascending dose tiers (≤25, 50 and ≥ 100 mg/kg; RR 0.88 → 0.67 → 0.41), and nano-encapsulated berberine markedly outperformed conventional berberine (kindling RR 0.04 vs 0.53). Mechanistically, berberine reduced lipid peroxidation (MDA, SMD 1.82, 0.63-3.01) and raised the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase (SOD, SMD 1.44, 0.48-2.40).

Conclusion

Berberine exerts a consistent, dose-dependent, multi-target anticonvulsant effect that is greatly enhanced by nanoformulation. Certainty was moderate for the primary outcome and low-moderate elsewhere, defining berberine as a rational candidate for further translational development in epilepsy.

raw.abstractText: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent chronic liver disorder, with its progressive form, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), characterized by steatosis, inflammation, hepatocyte injury, and fibrosis. However, the underlying mechanism remains incompletely understood. Here, we performed an in vivo CRISPR screen in Cas9 mice fed a methionine- and choline-deficient (MCD) diet to identify epigenetic regulators of MASH. SETDB1 emerged as a key modulator: hepatocyte-specific loss of Setdb1 exacerbated steatosis, inflammation, ductular reaction, and fibrosis, whereas Setdb1 overexpression markedly alleviated these pathological features. Notably, human liver samples showed decreased SETDB1 expression with advancing MASLD. Furthermore, SETDB1 deficiency increased hepatic ferroptosis by upregulating ACSL4, aggravating MASH pathology, whereas ACSL4 knockout reduced liver injury in the absence of SETDB1. SETDB1 overexpression protected against liver damage by repressing ACSL4. Therefore, the SETDB1-ACSL4-ferroptosis axis regulates MASH progression and represents a potential therapeutic target.

raw.abstractText:
Objective

Arterial serum was generally used to uncover shifts in the metabolic profile induced by surgery and anaesthesia. The specific perioperative metabolic alterations in the brain remain largely unknown. We aimed to detect perioperative changes in cerebral metabolism by arteriovenous gradients of circulating metabolites across the brain using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis.

Methods

The prospective study was conducted at Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital, China. Twenty patients with unilateral pulmonary lesion were recruited. Patients undergoing thoracic surgery were randomised to receive general anaesthesia with sevoflurane or propofol. Blood samples from radial artery and jugular bulb were collected before and after first anaesthetic administration, at the end of 60 min of maintenance of anaesthesia and 60 min after patients regained consciousness. LC-MS-based untargeted metabolomics strategies were used to determine the difference in abundance of circulating metabolites between artery and jugular bulb.

Results

A total of 3900 metabolites were detected. Potential critical alterations of metabolites including phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), choline, isocitrate and lactate and pathways were identified. Brain took up PC and PE in group sevoflurane but secreted these compounds in group propofol. Additionally, propofol was associated with the release of choline and isocitrate from brain. In both groups, lactic acid entered brain intraoperatively.

Conclusion

This work may offer a comprehensive mapping of perioperative alterations of cerebral metabolism in patients under general anaesthesia and a new direction for further studies in pharmacology of general anaesthetics and pathogenesis of perioperative brain dysfunction. raw.abstractText: Polysubstance use is a major contributor to neurotoxicity, yet the integrated redox-dependent mechanisms underlying polydrug exposure remain poorly understood. Cocaine (Coc), nicotine (Nic), and alcohol (Alc) are commonly co-abused substances associated with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuronal impairment. Here, we investigated the effects of Coc, Nic, Alc, Nic+Alc, and Coc+Nic+Alc exposure on redox homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and epigenetic regulation in mice brain and human microglial cells (HMC3). Individual and polydrug exposures increased reactive oxygen species, altered mitochondrial and antioxidant defense pathways, including GSS, SOD2, PGC-1α, TFAM, and Trx/TXNIP signaling. Polydrug exposure further reduced oxidative phosphorylation complexes, altered NRF1/NRF2-mediated mitochondrial pathways, and decreased Mfn1/2 expression in mice brain tissue, consistent with impaired mitochondrial function and fusion. In HMC3 cells, polysubstance exposure similarly increased oxidative stress, as demonstrated by MitoSOX, DHE, and DCFH-DA assays. These redox and mitochondrial alterations were accompanied by changes in DNMT and TET enzymes, consistent with altered epigenetic regulation. Behaviorally, both individual and polydrug exposures produced significant conditioned place preference. Notably, polydrug exposure was associated with reduced tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactivity in the substantia nigra, along with altered dopamine transporter and dopamine D2 receptor expression, increased caspase-3 activation and ASC expression, and changes in microglial P2RY12 expression, together with enhanced neuroinflammatory responses. Collectively, these findings identify interconnected redox, mitochondrial, and epigenetic alterations associated with polysubstance-induced neuroadaptation and neurotoxicity. Although selected molecular pathways exhibited partial counter-regulation, persistent mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammatory responses, and alterations in dopaminergic markers were observed following polysubstance exposure, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for substance use disorders.

raw.abstractText: Creatine is among the most extensively studied and widely used nutritional supplements in sports and exercise science. Over the past two decades, however, interest has expanded well beyond skeletal muscle, driven by growing recognition of the central role played by the creatine-phosphocreatine system in cerebral bioenergetics. Experimental evidence indicates that creatine contributes to neuronal energy homeostasis, mitochondrial function, membrane stability and potentially neuroprotection. This has fuelled growing enthusiasm for the idea that creatine supplementation might enhance cognitive function and benefit individuals with compromised cerebral metabolism. Yet, despite strong physiological plausibility, clinical findings remain inconsistent and often difficult to interpret. In this review, it is argued that the gap between proposed mechanisms and available clinical evidence reflects two distinct challenges: biological constraints on cerebral creatine availability after supplementation, and persistent methodological weaknesses in the clinical literature. We contend that the central challenge for the coming decade is not to identify new mechanisms of creatine action in the brain, but to establish, unequivocally, whether measurable changes in cerebral bioenergetics translate into meaningful cognitive benefit - whether as enhanced performance in healthy individuals or as clinically significant improvement in patient populations.

raw.abstractText: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex, progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which amyloid-β accumulation, tau dysregulation, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, synaptic loss and neurodegeneration interact to drive memory loss and cognitive decline. Despite advances in symptomatic therapies and anti-amyloid agents, clinical benefit remains modest, supporting interest in polypharmacological approaches. Cannabidiol (CBD) is a non-psychotropic phytocannabinoid that interacts with several signalling systems relevant to AD, including cannabinoid-related pathways, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ), transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channels, 5-HT1A signalling, fatty acid-binding proteins involved in anandamide transport, GPR55 and adenosine transporters. The most consistent preclinical findings indicate that CBD attenuates neuroinflammatory and oxidative responses and improves selected behavioural outcomes. Evidence for amyloid-related effects is supportive but heterogeneous. Direct evidence for tau modulation has expanded in transgenic and chemically induced models, but findings remain model-dependent, whereas mitochondrial rescue and adult hippocampal neurogenesis are less firmly established. Methodological variability in CBD source, formulation, dose, route, treatment window, sex, age and outcome selection limits direct comparison between studies. Work on other cannabinoids and CBD:Δ9-THC combinations is discussed for context, and current evidence does not establish CBD as a disease-modifying treatment in AD. Overall, current preclinical evidence supports continued investigation of CBD as a multi-target neuroprotective candidate in AD, provided that future studies use standardized, mechanism-focused and translationally relevant designs. This review compares preclinical evidence across pathological domains and identifies translational research priorities.

raw.abstractText: Cyclic diguanylate (c-di-GMP) is an ubiquitous second messenger in bacteria. Intracellular levels and/or local pools of this molecule modulate a diversity of processes in response to environmental and metabolic signals, including the transition between the motile unicellular mode of life and the biofilm lifestyle. Proteins involved in the synthesis and degradation of this second messenger, and in the response to c-di-GMP, have been characterized in different species, but there are still significant knowledge gaps, particularly in less studied bacteria. In this work, we have focused on a predicted diguanylate cyclase of Stutzerimonas stutzeri MJL19 containing a periplasmic ligand binding domain. This protein, which we have named RmcM, binds two structurally similar amino acid derivatives, γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and 5-aminovaleric acid, with high affinity, modulating c-di-GMP contents in response to these two ligands. Deletion of rcmM caused an increase of motility, while surprisingly also leading to a transient increase in global second messenger under some environmental conditions. In contrast, rmcM in a multicopy plasmid leads to increased c-di-GMP levels. In the course of this work, evidences were also obtained on the regulatory role of the alternative sigma factor RpoN on c-di-GMP turnover and the associated phenotypes in this strain.

raw.abstractText: To explore the feasibility of using coal gasification slag (CGS) as a substitute for limestone filler (LF) in asphalt mastic, six representative CGS powders and one commonly used LF were selected. The physicochemical properties of the CGS powders and the rheological properties of the corresponding asphalt mastics were investigated, and an economic evaluation was conducted. Through comparative analysis of the high- and low-temperature rheological properties of the asphalt mastics at a fixed filler-to-binder (F/B) ratio of 1.0 by mass, low-carbon gasification slag generated by the pulverized-coal process (coded as LCPGS) was identified as the preferred raw material, achieving the optimal balance between high- and low-temperature properties. Compared with LF asphalt mastic, LCPGS asphalt mastic (LCPGS-AM) showed a 19.4% higher G*/sinδ at 64 °C, while m/S value at −12 °C was only 2.2% lower. Based on the rheological and fatigue-resistance properties of LCPGS-AMs with different F/B ratios, a suitable F/B range of 30%–40% by volume was determined, which can serve as a reference for asphalt mastic and mixture design. Complete replacement of conventional LF with LCPGS can reduce material cost by approximately 56.3%, yielding significant economic benefits. The preliminary performance and economic analyses indicate that the use of CGS powder as an alternative filler in asphalt mixtures is feasible.

payload.title: Creatine and cognitive function: Why has physiological plausibility not translated into convincing clinical evidence?
payload.abstract: Creatine is among the most extensively studied and widely used nutritional supplements in sports and exercise science. Over the past two decades, however, interest has expanded well beyond skeletal muscle, driven by growing recognition of the central role played by the creatine-phosphocreatine system in cerebral bioenergetics. Experimental evidence indicates that creatine contributes to neuronal energy homeostasis, mitochondrial function, membrane stability and potentially neuroprotection. This has fuelled growing enthusiasm for the idea that creatine supplementation might enhance cognitive function and benefit individuals with compromised cerebral metabolism. Yet, despite strong physiological plausibility, clinical findings remain inconsistent and often difficult to interpret. In this review, it is argued that the gap between proposed mechanisms and available clinical evidence reflects two distinct challenges: biological constraints on cerebral creatine availability after supplementation, and persistent methodological weaknesses in the clinical literature. We contend that the central challenge for the coming decade is not to identify new mechanisms of creatine action in the brain, but to establish, unequivocally, whether measurable changes in cerebral bioenergetics translate into meaningful cognitive benefit - whether as enhanced performance in healthy individuals or as clinically significant improvement in patient populations.
